title: Before and after
job: Time clauses: while, until, since, already, not yet
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: SANSKRIT BUILDS EVERY SUBORDINATE CLAUSE THE SAME WAY. A word beginning ya- opens the subordinate clause and says what kind of link it is; a word beginning ta- stands in the main clause and answers it. Learn the shape once and five different clauses come with it.

THE FIVE PAIRS, TOGETHER FOR THE FIRST TIME. yataḥ … ataḥ is cause (L1-M9), yaḥ … saḥ is the relative (L3-M2), yadi … tarhi is the condition (L3-M4), and this module adds yadā … tadā for time and yāvat … tāvat for extent. Same frame, five jobs.

THE ANSWERING WORD IS NOT EQUALLY OBLIGATORY, and a slogan here would be false of two of the five. L3-M2's saḥ may NEVER be dropped; L3-M4's tarhi MAY be; tāvat may not, because without it yāvat has nothing to measure. This course writes tadā every time.

yadā … tadā marks a POINT: when this happens, then that happens. yāvat … tāvat marks an EXTENT: for as long as this lasts, that lasts. yadā vṛṣṭiḥ asti is a moment of rain; yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti is the whole time it goes on.

THE ya- CLAUSE COMES FIRST AND COMPLETE, then the main clause. English lets the time clause go either way — 'I read at home when it rains' — so the Sanskrit sentence is the English one reversed, and the literal line shows the reversal rather than hiding it.

pūrvam is 'before · formerly' and paścāt is 'after · afterwards', and THIS MODULE USES THEM AS ADVERBS ONLY. In real Sanskrit both also stand behind a case-marked noun — bhojanāt paścāt, 'after the meal' — and that use is named here and written nowhere.

adhunā is 'now'. 'Still' is adhunā api: TWO separate words, adhunā and L1-M10's api, standing side by side. Neither of them changes shape, and nothing joins them — mama mitram adhunā api vidyālayam gacchati.

'NOT YET' IS WHERE THE DICTIONARY AND THIS COURSE PART. A dictionary prints the joined form, adya plus api run together. External sandhi is never written across a word boundary here, so this course writes na adya api — three words it has owned since L1, and no new word at all. The joined shape is in the sound line.

ENGLISH 'SINCE' IS TWO WORDS AND SANSKRIT SPLITS THEM. The clock sense is yadā or yāvat; the reason sense is L1-M9's yataḥ or L4-M2's ablative of cause. Translate 'since' the same way for both and you have written a reason where a time belonged.

WHAT THIS MODULE DOES NOT ADD. There is no separate word for 'already' here — the participial past carries it, and pūrvam supplies it when the sentence needs saying out loud. No clock and no calendar, deferred since L2-M6. No new sequencer: L2-M10's prathamam, tataḥ, anantaram and ante join whole SENTENCES, while these pairs join clauses inside one. And no new absolutive — L3-M1 owns those, and paścāt stands beside one rather than replacing it.

sentences.display: yadā vṛṣṭiḥ asti tadā aham gṛhe paṭhāmi.
sentences.script: यदा वृष्टिः अस्ति तदा अहम् गृहे पठामि।
sentences.cue: When it rains, I read at home.
sentences.literal: when rain is then I at-home read

words.note: 'When'. It opens the time clause and is answered by tadā in the main clause — the fifth ya- word this course has taught and the same frame as yadi and yaḥ.
L4-M2's rain in its naming shape. vṛṣṭiḥ asti is 'there is rain'; the 'because of' shape is vṛṣṭeḥ.
L1-M3's 'is · there is', here holding the time clause together.
'Then'. The ta- word that answers yadā. It marks the main clause, so it never starts the sentence — the ya- clause does.
L1-M1's 'I'. It sits in the MAIN clause, behind tadā, because the ya- clause is finished first.
L1-M6's house in its 'in' shape, which L1-M7 made the place case.
L1-M4's reading verb in the first singular. The -mi says who, so aham could be dropped.

sentences.trap: English says 'I read at home when it rains' and puts the clock second. Sanskrit puts the ya- clause FIRST, so the halves swap places on the way across.
sentences.sound: ya-DAA VRISH-tih AS-ti ta-DAA a-HAM GRI-heh pa-THAA-mi.

variations.display: yadā vṛṣṭiḥ asti tadā aham gṛhe na gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदा वृष्टिः अस्ति तदा अहम् गृहे न गच्छामि।
variations.cue: When it rains, I do not go home.
variations.changed: the main clause is negated, and the negation sits inside it — the time clause is untouched by a na in the other half

variations.display: yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti tāvat aham gṛhe paṭhāmi.
variations.script: यावत् वृष्टिः अस्ति तावत् अहम् गृहे पठामि।
variations.cue: As long as it rains, I read at home.
variations.changed: the pair is swapped and the meaning moves from a point to a stretch: yadā is the moment, yāvat is the whole duration

variations.display: yadā vṛṣṭiḥ asti tadā mama bhaginī gṛhe paṭhati.
variations.script: यदा वृष्टिः अस्ति तदा मम भगिनी गृहे पठति।
variations.cue: When it rains, my sister reads at home.
variations.changed: the main clause changes person and the verb follows it to -ti; nothing in the yadā clause moves

sentences.usage: The ordinary way to state a habit tied to a condition of the day.

sentences.display: yāvat aham paṭhāmi tāvat mama bhrātā likhati.
sentences.script: यावत् अहम् पठामि तावत् मम भ्राता लिखति।
sentences.cue: While I study, my brother writes.
sentences.literal: as-long-as I read so-long my brother writes

words.note: 'As long as'. It measures an EXTENT of time rather than a point, and is answered by tāvat, which may never be dropped.
L1-M1's 'I', here the subject of the yāvat clause rather than of the main one.
L1-M4's reading verb in the first singular, inside the subordinate clause — a ya- clause takes an ordinary finite verb.
'For that long'. The ta- word that answers yāvat. Drop it and yāvat has nothing to measure against, which is why this pair is the strict one.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L2-M2's brother in its naming shape, subject of the main clause.
L1-M4's writing verb in the third singular — the cell bhrātā, bhavān and saḥ all take.

sentences.trap: tāvat looks droppable because English drops 'so long'. It is not: yāvat with no tāvat behind it leaves the extent measured against nothing.
sentences.sound: YAA-vat a-HAM pa-THAA-mi TAA-vat MA-ma BHRAA-taa LI-kha-ti.

variations.display: yāvat aham paṭhāmi tāvat mama bhaginī likhati.
variations.script: यावत् अहम् पठामि तावत् मम भगिनी लिखति।
variations.cue: While I study, my sister writes.
variations.changed: the main clause's subject changes gender; likhati does not move, because a Sanskrit present tense marks person and not gender

variations.display: yāvat mama bhrātā likhati tāvat aham paṭhāmi.
variations.script: यावत् मम भ्राता लिखति तावत् अहम् पठामि।
variations.cue: While my brother writes, I study.
variations.changed: the two halves trade places — what was measured is now what measures, and each verb follows its own clause

variations.display: yāvat aham na paṭhāmi tāvat mama bhrātā na likhati.
variations.script: यावत् अहम् न पठामि तावत् मम भ्राता न लिखति।
variations.cue: As long as I do not study, my brother does not write.
variations.changed: both halves are negated; na stands in front of its own verb in each clause and never once for both

sentences.usage: Two things going on at the same time, in one breath.

sentences.display: yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti tāvat vayam na gacchāmaḥ.
sentences.script: यावत् वृष्टिः अस्ति तावत् वयम् न गच्छामः।
sentences.cue: As long as it is raining, we are not going.
sentences.literal: as-long-as rain is so-long we not go

words.note: 'As long as'. It measures an EXTENT of time rather than a point, and is answered by tāvat, which may never be dropped.
L4-M2's rain in its naming shape. Here it is what lasts, which is why yāvat and not yadā.
L1-M3's 'is · there is'.
'For that long'. The ta- word that answers yāvat. Drop it and yāvat has nothing to measure against, which is why this pair is the strict one.
L2-M6's 'we', subject of the main clause.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb it denies. It belongs to the main clause alone.
L2-M6's first-plural going verb. The -maḥ agrees with vayam, so the pronoun could be dropped.

variations.display: yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti tāvat vayam gṛhe paśyāmaḥ.
variations.script: यावत् वृष्टिः अस्ति तावत् वयम् गृहे पश्यामः।
variations.cue: As long as it is raining, we watch at home.
variations.changed: the main clause becomes positive and takes a different first-plural verb; the yāvat clause is untouched

variations.display: yadā vṛṣṭiḥ asti tadā vayam na gacchāmaḥ.
variations.script: यदा वृष्टिः अस्ति तदा वयम् न गच्छामः।
variations.cue: When it rains, we do not go.
variations.changed: the pair is swapped to yadā … tadā, which reads the rain as an occasion rather than as a stretch of time

variations.display: yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti tāvat bhavatā na gantavyam.
variations.script: यावत् वृष्टिः अस्ति तावत् भवता न गन्तव्यम्।
variations.cue: As long as it is raining, you must not go.
variations.changed: the main clause becomes L4-M1's gerundive, so the person who must not go moves into the instrumental and no nominative is left

mistake.display: yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti vayam na gacchāmaḥ.
mistake.why: tāvat has been dropped. yāvat measures, and with nothing to measure against the sentence reads as a bare 'while' hanging in the air. L3-M4's tarhi may go; tāvat may not.

sentences.usage: Said at a doorway, of a plan that is waiting on the weather.

sentences.display: aham bhojanam khāditvā paścāt pustakam paṭhāmi.
sentences.script: अहम् भोजनम् खादित्वा पश्चात् पुस्तकम् पठामि।
sentences.cue: After eating a meal, I read a book.
sentences.literal: I meal having-eaten afterwards book read

words.note: L1-M1's 'I', and the one subject of both halves — an absolutive needs the two actions to belong to the same person.
L2-M5's meal, as the thing eaten.
L3-M1's absolutive of khādati. It carries no person and no tense; the finite verb at the end carries both.
'Afterwards'. It stands in front of the clause that comes second, usually behind an absolutive: bhojanam khāditvā paścāt. It orders events inside ONE sentence.
L1-M1's book, as the thing read.
L1-M4's reading verb in the first singular, the only person-marked word in the sentence.

sentences.trap: paścāt does not replace the absolutive; it stands beside it. khāditvā already says the eating came first, and paścāt makes the order audible rather than supplying it.
sentences.sound: a-HAM bho-JA-nam khaa-dit-VAA pash-CHAAT pus-TA-kam pa-THAA-mi.

variations.display: aham bhojanam khāditvā paścāt pustakam na paṭhāmi.
variations.script: अहम् भोजनम् खादित्वा पश्चात् पुस्तकम् न पठामि।
variations.cue: After eating a meal, I do not read a book.
variations.changed: the finite verb is negated; the absolutive cannot be negated and stays exactly as it was

variations.display: aham bhojanam khāditvā paścāt pustakam paṭhitavān.
variations.script: अहम् भोजनम् खादित्वा पश्चात् पुस्तकम् पठितवान्।
variations.cue: After eating a meal, I read a book.
variations.changed: the finite verb becomes L1-M4's participial past, which is the only thing that had to move to put the whole sentence in the past

variations.display: aham pustakam paṭhitvā paścāt bhojanam khādāmi.
variations.script: अहम् पुस्तकम् पठित्वा पश्चात् भोजनम् खादामि।
variations.cue: After reading a book, I eat a meal.
variations.changed: the two actions trade places, and each verb trades shape with the other — the absolutive marks whichever came first

sentences.usage: The everyday way to put two of your own actions in order.
sentences.mnemonic: Absolutive first, paścāt says so out loud.

sentences.display: pūrvam aham saṃskṛtam na paṭhitavān, adhunā pratidinam paṭhāmi.
sentences.script: पूर्वम् अहम् संस्कृतम् न पठितवान्, अधुना प्रतिदिनम् पठामि।
sentences.cue: I did not study Sanskrit before; now I study every day.
sentences.literal: formerly I Sanskrit not studied, now every-day I-study

words.note: 'Formerly'. An adverb here and nothing else: it stands in front of its clause. Sanskrit also puts it behind a case-marked noun, and this course does not.
L1-M1's 'I'. It appears once, in the first half; the -mi of the second half already says who.
L1-M1's Sanskrit, as the thing studied in both halves.
L1-M2's 'not', denying the participle behind it and nothing in the other half.
L1-M4's participial past, agreeing with the speaker's gender. A woman says paṭhitavatī and the whole sentence forks there.
'Now'. With L1-M10's api behind it — adhunā api — it means 'still'. The two stay two words.
L1-M4's 'daily'. A frequency word is what turns a plain present into a habit.
L1-M4's reading verb in the first singular, carrying the 'now' half.

sentences.sound: POOR-vam a-HAM sans-KRI-tam na pa-thi-ta-VAAN, a-dhu-NAA pra-ti-DI-nam pa-THAA-mi.

variations.display: pūrvam aham saṃskṛtam na paṭhitavatī, adhunā pratidinam paṭhāmi.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् संस्कृतम् न पठितवती, अधुना प्रतिदिनम् पठामि।
variations.cue: I did not study Sanskrit before; now I study every day.
variations.changed: a woman speaks: only the participle moves, because the past forks at the speaker's gender and the present does not

variations.display: pūrvam aham saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān, adhunā na paṭhāmi.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् संस्कृतम् पठितवान्, अधुना न पठामि।
variations.cue: I used to study Sanskrit; now I do not.
variations.changed: the negation moves from the first half to the second, which turns a beginning into a stopping

variations.display: adhunā api aham saṃskṛtam paṭhāmi.
variations.script: अधुना अपि अहम् संस्कृतम् पठामि।
variations.cue: I still study Sanskrit.
variations.changed: the two halves collapse into one and adhunā takes api behind it, which is how this course says 'still'

sentences.usage: A then-and-now in one sentence, which is what a whole module will be built on later.

sentences.display: aham pustakam na adya api paṭhitavān.
sentences.script: अहम् पुस्तकम् न अद्य अपि पठितवान्।
sentences.cue: I have not read the book yet.
sentences.literal: I book not today even read

words.note: L1-M1's 'I', and the gender the participle at the end agrees with.
L1-M1's book, as the thing read.
L1-M2's 'not'. It is the first of the three words that together mean 'not yet'.
L1-M4's 'today'. Inside this phrase it is not about today at all — the three words together mean 'not yet'.
L1-M10's api, standing behind the word it leans on, exactly as L1-M10 taught. 'Not even today' is 'not yet'.
L1-M4's participial past. A woman says paṭhitavatī.

sentences.trap: A dictionary prints adya and api joined into one word, and copying that would mint a spelling this course does not own. The three words stay three.
sentences.sound: a-HAM PUS-ta-kam NAAD-yaa-pi pa-thi-ta-VAAN — the three words run together in speech as naadyaapi, and are written apart.

variations.display: aham pustakam na adya api paṭhitavatī.
variations.script: अहम् पुस्तकम् न अद्य अपि पठितवती।
variations.cue: I have not read the book yet.
variations.changed: a woman speaks; only the participle moves, and the three-word phrase is untouched by gender

variations.display: aham pustakam adhunā api paṭhāmi.
variations.script: अहम् पुस्तकम् अधुना अपि पठामि।
variations.cue: I am still reading the book.
variations.changed: 'not yet' becomes 'still': adhunā api with a present, against na adya api with a past participle

variations.display: kim bhavān pustakam na adya api paṭhitavān?
variations.script: किम् भवान् पुस्तकम् न अद्य अपि पठितवान्?
variations.cue: Have you not read the book yet?
variations.changed: L1-M2's kim turns it into a question and the speaker becomes the listener, so the participle agrees with bhavān

mistake.why: 'Not yet' has been taken apart and adya sent to the end as a plain 'today'. That says 'I did not read the book today', which is about one day and not about a thing still undone.

sentences.usage: Said of something you mean to finish and have not.
sentences.mnemonic: Not even today: three words, one meaning.

sentences.display: mama mitram adhunā api vidyālayam gacchati.
sentences.script: मम मित्रम् अधुना अपि विद्यालयम् गच्छति।
sentences.cue: My friend still goes to school.
sentences.literal: my friend now even school goes

words.note: L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L2-M2's friend. It is neuter, so nothing in the sentence agrees with it in the masculine.
'Now'. With L1-M10's api behind it — adhunā api — it means 'still'. The two stay two words.
L1-M10's api behind adhunā. The two together are 'still', and they stay two words.
L1-M6's school, as the destination — the accusative marks it and no word for 'to' is written.
L1-M2's going verb in the third singular.

variations.display: mama mitram adhunā api vidyālayam na gacchati.
variations.script: मम मित्रम् अधुना अपि विद्यालयम् न गच्छति।
variations.cue: My friend still does not go to school.
variations.changed: the verb is negated and 'still' survives in front of it — adhunā api leans on the whole clause, not on the verb alone

variations.display: mama mitram pūrvam vidyālayam gatavān.
variations.script: मम मित्रम् पूर्वम् विद्यालयम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: My friend used to go to school.
variations.changed: 'still' becomes 'formerly' and the present becomes the participial past; the destination is the only thing untouched

variations.display: kim mama mitram adhunā api vidyālayam gacchati?
variations.script: किम् मम मित्रम् अधुना अपि विद्यालयम् गच्छति?
variations.cue: Does my friend still go to school?
variations.changed: L1-M2's kim at the front makes a question of it and nothing else in the sentence moves

sentences.usage: Said of a state of affairs you half expected to have ended.

sentences.display: yadā mama pitā kāryālayam gacchati tadā aham vidyālayam gacchāmi.
sentences.script: यदा मम पिता कार्यालयम् गच्छति तदा अहम् विद्यालयम् गच्छामि।
sentences.cue: When my father goes to the office, I go to school.
sentences.literal: when my father office goes then I school go

words.note: 'When'. It opens the time clause and is answered by tadā in the main clause — the fifth ya- word this course has taught and the same frame as yadi and yaḥ.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape, inside the yadā clause.
L2-M2's father in his naming shape, subject of the subordinate clause.
L3-M8's office, as the destination.
L1-M2's going verb in the third singular, agreeing with pitā.
'Then'. The ta- word that answers yadā. It marks the main clause, so it never starts the sentence — the ya- clause does.
L1-M1's 'I', subject of the main clause and of nothing before tadā.
L1-M6's school, as the destination.
L1-M2's going verb in the first singular. Two clauses, two subjects, two person endings.

sentences.sound: ya-DAA MA-ma pi-TAA KAAR-yaa-la-yam GACH-cha-ti ta-DAA a-HAM vid-YAA-la-yam gach-CHAA-mi.

variations.display: yadā mama pitā kāryālayam gacchati tadā aham gṛhe paṭhāmi.
variations.script: यदा मम पिता कार्यालयम् गच्छति तदा अहम् गृहे पठामि।
variations.cue: When my father goes to the office, I read at home.
variations.changed: the main clause changes altogether; a ya- clause is finished before the main clause starts, so nothing in it has to move

variations.display: yadā mama pitā kāryālayam gatavān tadā aham vidyālayam gatavān.
variations.script: यदा मम पिता कार्यालयम् गतवान् तदा अहम् विद्यालयम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: When my father went to the office, I went to school.
variations.changed: both verbs become participial pasts; yadā … tadā does not change shape for tense, because it is not a verb

variations.display: yadā mama pitā kāryālayam na gacchati tadā aham api na gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदा मम पिता कार्यालयम् न गच्छति तदा अहम् अपि न गच्छामि।
variations.cue: When my father does not go to the office, I do not go either.
variations.changed: both halves are negated and api lands behind aham, which is L1-M10's placement and not a second 'still'

mistake.display: aham vidyālayam gacchāmi yadā mama pitā kāryālayam gacchati.
mistake.why: The English order has been kept. The ya- clause is what opens a Sanskrit sentence, and a tadā that never arrives leaves the main clause unanswered.

sentences.usage: Two daily routines pinned to each other.

sentences.display: aham kāryālayam gatvā paścāt gṛham gamiṣyāmi.
sentences.script: अहम् कार्यालयम् गत्वा पश्चात् गृहम् गमिष्यामि।
sentences.cue: Having gone to the office, I will go home afterwards.
sentences.literal: I office having-gone afterwards home will-go

words.note: L1-M1's 'I', and the single subject both actions belong to.
L3-M8's office, as the first destination.
L3-M1's absolutive of gacchati. It takes no tense of its own, so the future at the end covers both actions.
'Afterwards'. It stands in front of the clause that comes second, usually behind an absolutive: bhojanam khāditvā paścāt. It orders events inside ONE sentence.
L1-M6's house, as the second destination.
L1-M2's simple future in the first singular. It is the only word here that says when.

variations.display: aham kāryālayam gatvā paścāt gṛham gatavān.
variations.script: अहम् कार्यालयम् गत्वा पश्चात् गृहम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: Having gone to the office, I went home afterwards.
variations.changed: the future becomes the participial past, and the absolutive in front of it does not move — that is what tenselessness means

variations.display: aham kāryālayam gatvā paścāt gṛham gamiṣyāmi vā?
variations.script: अहम् कार्यालयम् गत्वा पश्चात् गृहम् गमिष्यामि वा?
variations.cue: Shall I go to the office and then go home?
variations.changed: L2-M9's vā turns the plan into an open question without touching the order of the two legs

variations.display: aham gṛham gatvā paścāt kāryālayam gamiṣyāmi.
variations.script: अहम् गृहम् गत्वा पश्चात् कार्यालयम् गमिष्यामि।
variations.cue: Having gone home, I will go to the office afterwards.
variations.changed: the two destinations trade places, which is the whole meaning of the sentence and costs one swap

sentences.usage: The ordinary way to lay out the rest of your day.

sentences.display: aham bhojanam pūrvam khāditavān, adhunā na khādāmi.
sentences.script: अहम् भोजनम् पूर्वम् खादितवान्, अधुना न खादामि।
sentences.cue: I have already eaten; I am not eating now.
sentences.literal: I meal before ate, now not I-eat

words.note: L1-M1's 'I'. It stands once and covers both halves.
L2-M5's meal, as the thing eaten.
'Formerly'. An adverb here and nothing else: it stands in front of its clause. Sanskrit also puts it behind a case-marked noun, and this course does not.
L1-M4's participial past. With pūrvam in front it is 'already ate'; this course has no separate word for 'already'.
'Now'. With L1-M10's api behind it — adhunā api — it means 'still'. The two stay two words.
L1-M2's 'not', denying the second half alone.
L1-M4's eating verb in the first singular.

sentences.trap: There is no word here for 'already'. The participial past carries it, and pūrvam only makes the order explicit — reaching for a separate word finds nothing.
sentences.sound: a-HAM bho-JA-nam POOR-vam khaa-di-ta-VAAN, a-dhu-NAA na khaa-DAA-mi.

variations.display: aham bhojanam pūrvam khāditavatī, adhunā na khādāmi.
variations.script: अहम् भोजनम् पूर्वम् खादितवती, अधुना न खादामि।
variations.cue: I have already eaten; I am not eating now.
variations.changed: a woman speaks, so the participle alone forks; the present in the second half is the same word for either speaker

variations.display: aham bhojanam pūrvam khāditavān, adhunā api khādāmi.
variations.script: अहम् भोजनम् पूर्वम् खादितवान्, अधुना अपि खादामि।
variations.cue: I ate before, and I am still eating.
variations.changed: na becomes api, which flips the second half from a stop to a continuation — adhunā api is 'still'

variations.display: aham bhojanam na adya api khāditavān.
variations.script: अहम् भोजनम् न अद्य अपि खादितवान्।
variations.cue: I have not eaten yet.
variations.changed: the whole thing becomes its opposite with the three-word 'not yet', which is the other end of this module

sentences.usage: The polite refusal at a table: you have eaten, so you are not eating.

comprehensionPool.display: yadā aham khādāmi tadā mama bhrātā paṭhati.
comprehensionPool.script: यदा अहम् खादामि तदा मम भ्राता पठति।
comprehensionPool.cue: When I eat, my brother reads.

comprehensionPool.display: yāvat bhavān atra asti tāvat aham na gamiṣyāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: यावत् भवान् अत्र अस्ति तावत् अहम् न गमिष्यामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: As long as you are here, I will not go.

comprehensionPool.display: pūrvam mama pitā kāryālayam gatavān, adhunā gṛhe asti.
comprehensionPool.script: पूर्वम् मम पिता कार्यालयम् गतवान्, अधुना गृहे अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: My father used to go to the office; now he is at home.

comprehensionPool.display: aham jalam pītvā paścāt bhojanam khādāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: अहम् जलम् पीत्वा पश्चात् भोजनम् खादामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: After drinking water, I eat a meal.

comprehensionPool.display: mama bhaginī adhunā api saṃskṛtam paṭhati.
comprehensionPool.script: मम भगिनी अधुना अपि संस्कृतम् पठति।

comprehensionPool.display: aham patram na adya api likhitavān.
comprehensionPool.script: अहम् पत्रम् न अद्य अपि लिखितवान्।
comprehensionPool.cue: I have not written the letter yet.

comprehensionPool.display: yadā bhavatī gacchati tadā aham api gacchāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: यदा भवती गच्छति तदा अहम् अपि गच्छामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: When you go, I go too.

comprehensionPool.display: yāvat aham na paṭhāmi tāvat mama mātā na santuṣṭā.
comprehensionPool.script: यावत् अहम् न पठामि तावत् मम माता न सन्तुष्टा।
comprehensionPool.cue: As long as I do not study, my mother is not pleased.
Now we are going to the temple.

comprehensionPool.display: aham kāryam kṛtvā paścāt miṣṭānnam khāditavān.
comprehensionPool.script: अहम् कार्यम् कृत्वा पश्चात् मिष्टान्नम् खादितवान्।
comprehensionPool.cue: Having finished the work, I ate sweets afterwards.

comprehensionPool.display: yadā utsavaḥ asti tadā janāḥ mandiram gacchanti.
comprehensionPool.script: यदा उत्सवः अस्ति तदा जनाः मन्दिरम् गच्छन्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: When there is a festival, people go to the temple.

comprehensionPool.display: mama bhrātā pūrvam atra paṭhitavān, adhunā kāryālaye asti.
comprehensionPool.script: मम भ्राता पूर्वम् अत्र पठितवान्, अधुना कार्यालये अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: My brother used to study here; now he is at the office.

comprehensionPool.display: yāvat vṛṣṭiḥ asti tāvat mārgaḥ na uttamaḥ.
comprehensionPool.script: यावत् वृष्टिः अस्ति तावत् मार्गः न उत्तमः।
comprehensionPool.cue: As long as it is raining, the road is not good.
